source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: Meta-analysis of the link between the c factor and an outside group-performance task. The effect is moderate but very uneven across studies.
numbers: 8 independent samples, N = 857 groups, 9 criterion tasks. Random-effects r = .26 (95% CI .10 to .40). Q(8) = 59.36, p < .001, I2 = 86.5%, tau2 = .05. Fail-safe N = 96. Egger p = .124.
quote: We caution against prematurely embracing notions of the c- factor unless it can be independently and robustly replicated
limits: Only 8 samples, fewer than the 10 needed to judge funnel asymmetry. All but one sample came from the Woolley group. Criterion tasks differ in every study.
agent_relevance: Even the friendly estimate is r near .26 with huge heterogeneity. Do not treat c as a stable predictor of how well a group of agents will do on a new task.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: Average member IQ barely predicted group performance in the subset of studies that measured it, but the estimate is imprecise. The c-versus-g comparison is therefore not settled.
numbers: 5 independent samples, N = 366 groups. Mean member IQ to criterion r = .06 (95% CI -.08 to .20). I2 = 35%, Q(5) = 7.72, p = .17. Earlier meta-analyses (Bell 2007, Devine and Philips 2001, Stewart 2006) pooled r = .28 (95% CI .25 to .30). About 80% of studies lacked power to detect the main correlations.
limits: Only four studies (five samples) controlled for member IQ at all. Wide CI includes the older .28 value.
agent_relevance: c has not been shown to add validity beyond g. Individual ability stays the default predictor to test against.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: The first-factor variance claim holds on the surface (about 43%) but the factor is weak when measured as average variance extracted (AVE).
numbers: First factor explained a mean of 43% (SD 3.6%) of total variance across samples. AVE per sample 22.26% to 36.50%. Mean AVE 30.23% across 49 loadings. Common 50% cut-off not met. The authors note g in their own ICAR-16 sample also had AVE of about 30%.
limits: The 50% AVE cut-off is a convention. The AVE of 44% in Riedl 2021 was later corrected to 19.6% (see b07). Rowe shows AVE near 30% in other samples.
agent_relevance: A '40% of variance' headline can be total variance, not common variance. Check which figure a paper reports before quoting it.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: The c to g link is small and differs by who ran the study. Independent labs found a larger overlap than the original lab.
numbers: c to mean member IQ r = .19 over 5 samples (345 groups). Two independent studies r = .32. Woolley-affiliated studies r = .10. Positive manifold: 163 of 171 inter-task correlations positive (95%). 59% between 0 and .30, 28% between .30 and .50, 8% at .50 or more.
limits: Tiny samples. Barlow's studies had the negative and near-zero task correlations. Brainstorming and shopping tasks have little validity as IQ tasks.
agent_relevance: A positive manifold exists but is mostly low to moderate. The 'general' part is thin.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: Replication scorecard from the review: attempts by independent authors partly or fully failed; attempts by the original lab all succeeded.
numbers: 19 independent samples, 1359 groups of 2 to 6 members. Only 7 of 19 samples independent of Woolley and co-authors. Mean 6.3 subtests. Mean first factor 43.03%. Mean c to criterion r = .253.
quote: All attempts to reproduce the c- factor under independent authorship either partially or completely failed
limits: Authors' own coding. Several samples are unpublished theses. Search ended November 2019.
agent_relevance: Treat positive replications from the originating lab as weaker evidence. Prefer independent tests when judging a scaffold idea built on c.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups, PNAS 118(21):e2005737118
finding: Large pooled data from 22 studies of group tasks. One factor was found, with modest loadings. Collaboration process predicted it more than member skill.
numbers: 22 studies, 5,279 individuals, 1,356 groups of 2 to 7. 8 task types, each study used 4 to 8. Mean inter-item r = .27 (range .12 to .50). Loadings .27 to .52. Leave-one-task-out prediction mean r = .40 (95% CI .26 to .53). 1 SD higher CI went with about 18% (plus or minus 12%) higher task performance. Sudoku: over 51% of explained variation was individual skill. Unscramble Words: 55% was group process.
limits: Secondary analysis. The text read here has no limitations section. Predictor models are exploratory OLS. Tasks are short lab tasks. Printed AVE of 44% was wrong (b07).
agent_relevance: Evidence for some cross-task generality in human groups. The strongest lever is process (skill congruence, strategy), not raw skill. Task type changes which lever matters.

source: Correction for Riedl et al., PNAS 119(19):e2204380119 (2022)
finding: The average variance extracted in Riedl 2021 was wrong because of a software error. The corrected value is 19.6%, not 44%. Model fit statistics were also redone.
numbers: AVE 44% corrected to 19.6%. Model 1 (3 tasks) is saturated, 0 df, so fit is not informative. Model 2 (5 tasks): chi2(5, N=1,356) = 19.514, p = .002, CFI = .93, RMSEA = .046. Model 4 (8 tasks): chi2(20) = 93.284, CFI = .833, RMSEA = .052. Old figure for Model 4 was chi2(28) = 466.8.
quote: due to a mistake in a software package, the average variance extracted (AVE) for the factor analyses reported in SI Appendix, Table S4 are incorrect
limits: The correction text lists the AVE and fit changes only. Loadings of .27 to .52 stay. It does not touch the leave-one-out r = .40.
agent_relevance: A published 'one factor, 44%' claim fell to about a fifth of indicator variance. Re-check numbers when a result will drive design. Generality is weaker than first stated.

source: Credé and Howardson (2017) The structure of group task performance: a second look at collective intelligence, J Applied Psychology 102(10):1483-1492
finding: Reanalysis of six samples from the Woolley 2010 line. They concluded that a general factor does not explain much variation across a wide range of group tasks and that artifacts may inflate it.
numbers: 6 samples re-analysed (Rowe 2021 gives N = 487 groups pooled). Press summary: only one of six, an Indiana University 2014 study, drew the no-c conclusion. Rowe 2021 quotes the paper: data do not support the inference that a general factor can explain substantial variation across a wide cross-section of group tasks.
limits: I read a press summary (ScienceDaily) and Rowe's description, not the paper PDF. No coefficients available here. Woolley, Kim and Malone (2018) replied that the data do not support the artifact explanation (SSRN page was blocked, so only known via a search snippet).
agent_relevance: Mechanisms offered: low effort by one group, one member doing the work, averaging of individual answers. These match failure modes in agent ensembles where outputs are just averaged.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence, Intelligence 60
finding: Three replications found a general group factor but showed it came from individual IQ. The women, turn-taking and social-sensitivity predictors mostly failed.
numbers: 3 studies, 312 people (groups of 3: 26 groups in study 1, 40 in study 2, 40 in study 3). Factor explained 39.8% (study 1) and about 50% (study 2). Study 1 regression: R2 = .57, mean IQ beta = .76 (p < .001), proportion female beta = .12 (ns), RME beta = -.11 (ns). Study 2 model R2 = .85, IQ beta = .74. Joint SEM of studies 2 and 3: individual IQ accounted for about 100% of latent group-IQ. The abstract also says about 80% of group-IQ differences.
quote: Smart groups are (simply) groups of smart people.
limits: Small groups of 3, small samples, short lab tasks. The authors address a power criticism in the paper. IQ measure was the Wonderlic, as in Woolley study 2.
agent_relevance: Direct rival explanation: c is mainly a sum of member ability. For an agent group, check how much of the group score is just the strength of the underlying model.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people
finding: Reading the Mind in the Eyes (RME) was linked to group-IQ in one study by simple regression, but a structural model showed it affected only one task, not the latent factor.
numbers: Study 2: RME beta = .30 [.11, .50], p = .003 in regression. Joint SEM of studies 2 and 3: RME had no effect on the latent factor. Number of women and turn-taking: no support in any of the 3 studies, and signs sometimes wrong.
limits: Regression and latent-variable analysis disagree, so the method choice decides the story.
agent_relevance: The 'social sensitivity' lever may be a task-specific effect. Do not build a scaffold step on it without a task-level test.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris and Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? PLOS ONE 9(12):e115212
finding: A general factor appeared in both face-to-face and online text-chat groups, and group RME predicted it in both. This was a supportive result from the original lab.
numbers: 68 groups of 4 (272 people), 32 face-to-face, 36 online. First factor 49% (face-to-face) and 41% (online). Group RME to c: r = .53 (p = .002) and r = .55 (p < .001). Without 2 outlier groups r = .47 and .48. Proportion of women to c online r = .41 (p = .01), mediated by RME.
limits: Temporary one-session groups from Boston. Correlational. Funded by Cisco via the MIT Center for Collective Intelligence. Barlow and Dennis (2016) did not find a dominant factor in virtual text groups (b12).
agent_relevance: Social sensitivity can matter even without voice or faces. Weak support only, since independent replications did not agree (b04, b08).

source: Barlow and Dennis (2016) as tabulated in Rowe et al. (2021)
finding: Independent test in virtual text-based groups did not find a dominant factor; the c factor did not predict a profit-maximisation task.
numbers: 86 groups. First factor 42%. Only 50% of task correlations positive. c to criterion r = .07 (p > .05). Barlow 2015 thesis: control group factor 33%, experimental group 46% with c to criterion r = .339, p = .026 in the experimental group only.
limits: Second-hand through Rowe 2021 Tables 1 to 3. I did not open the Barlow paper itself. Only 3 tasks, partly of low validity.
agent_relevance: c may not appear when tasks are few or low in validity. A 3-task 'general factor' is fragile.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) as tabulated in Rowe et al. (2021)
finding: The original Science paper numbers as re-tabulated: a first factor of 43 to 44% and a c to criterion link that shrank from study 1 to study 2.
numbers: Study 1: 40 groups, 43.4% first factor, c to criterion r = .52, c to mean member IQ r = .19 (ns). Study 2: 152 groups, 44.1%, r = .28, c to IQ r = .15 (p = .04). Task correlations 100% and 93% positive.
limits: Numbers are secondary (Rowe Table 1). I did not open the Science paper.
agent_relevance: The headline effect (r = .52) came from the smallest study of 40 groups. Expect shrinkage on replication.

source: Rowe et al. (2024) and Graf et al. (2019) as described in the 2025 dyadic CI paper
finding: Competing structures. A Gf-Gc style battery gave two factors rather than one. A meta-analysis suggested three factors: idea generation, conflict resolution, task execution.
numbers: Rowe 2024: two factors fit better than one. Graf 2019: 3-factor structure. LePine 2008 (138 studies) found a second-order team-process model with three broad processes. No effect sizes in the text read here.
limits: Second-hand description. I did not open the Rowe 2024 or Graf 2019 papers.
agent_relevance: A single scalar group ability is too coarse. Keep separate checks for generation, conflict handling and execution.

source: Dyadic collective intelligence study, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (2025), doi 10.1186/s41235-025-00655-0
finding: In dyads on well-structured tasks, individual intelligence and confidence were the strongest predictors of collective intelligence. Social sensitivity replicated; turn-taking and gender composition did not.
numbers: 105 undergraduate dyads, 3 CHC-aligned group tasks. Hierarchical regression block 3: individual intelligence beta = .33 (p < .01), confidence beta = .32 (p < .001), added 25% of variance (delta R2 = .25). Social sensitivity beta fell from .39 to .22. Final R2 = .60. Turn-taking beta = .08 (ns). One-factor CFA fit poorly (RMSEA .25, CFI .81) while a two-factor intelligence-plus-confidence model fit well (RMSEA .02, CFI .99).
quote: individual intelligence and confidence were the strongest predictors of dyadic CI for well-structured tasks
limits: Dyads only. Well-structured tasks. Undergraduates. The authors say it is not a full account of CI.
agent_relevance: Task type is a boundary condition: on well-defined problems, ability and calibrated confidence dominate. Fits a solver agent where confidence handling matters.

source: Dyadic collective intelligence study, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (2025)
finding: Three dyad profiles appeared: high on both individual and collective scores, low on both, and better collectively than alone.
numbers: Latent profile analysis, N = 105 dyads, 3 profiles. Group differences small to moderate, partial eta squared .06 to .15. Number of females F(2,96) = 3.91, p = .02. Working memory F(2,96) = 8.43, p < .001, partial eta2 = .15.
limits: Small N. Profiles are data-driven and not validated outside the sample.
agent_relevance: Not every group gains from working together. Only one profile beat its members, so a scaffold should test for gain rather than assume it.

source: Kommol, Riedl and Woolley (2025) The structure of collective intelligence: evidence for collective memory, attention, and reasoning (PsyArXiv preprint)
finding: A preprint by the original line of authors reanalyses the 22-study data and argues that a hierarchical three-factor model (memory, attention, reasoning) fits better than a single factor, mostly in established groups.
numbers: 22 studies, 5,279 individuals, 1,356 groups, same data as Riedl 2021. Fit indices were not on the page I read.
limits: Abstract only. Preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I could see. Same authors as the original c work.
agent_relevance: Even the proponents now move away from a single c. Memory, attention and reasoning map loosely to retrieval, focus and inference steps in an agent.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models, Intelligence
finding: Individual LLMs show a positive manifold and a general ability factor across tests, tied to parameter count.
numbers: 591 LLMs, 12 tests. Strong positive manifold and one general factor. A combined knowledge and reading-writing group factor. Parameter count correlated positively with the general factor, with diminishing returns.
limits: Abstract only (via Semantic Scholar). Authors say it may reflect achievement or expertise more than intelligence.
agent_relevance: A general factor among LLMs is cheap to get because models differ in size. This is the confound for any group c of LLM groups (b19).

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying collective intelligence factor in LLM agent groups for generalizable multi-agent system design, Findings of ACL
finding: A general factor was reported across 108 LLM agent groups on 5 tasks. It was much stronger than in human groups.
numbers: 108 groups from 8 LLMs, sizes 3, 5 or 8, 2 or 3 rounds, 3 topologies, homogeneous or mixed. 5 tasks (commonsense, math, game, coding, writing). Mean task r = .55 (human groups .28). First factor 66.3% of variance, second 18.7%. One-factor CFA chi2 = 30.6, CFI = .967. Leave-one-task-out r above .8 on 3 tasks, about .5 on the others (all p < .001).
limits: The factor is not controlled for base-model strength (members range from 7B to 72B models). One debate-style framework only. Groups under 10 agents. No independent replication known.
agent_relevance: c-style numbers are easy to produce with LLM groups, which likely reflects shared model strength. Do not read it as proof of a transferable group trait.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) ACI factor paper
finding: Regression and random-forest analysis of what predicts the LLM group factor. Collaboration process mattered most, then model ability, with group size small.
numbers: Random forest: skill congruence over 50% of total importance, mean member ability 37%, max ability, group size and effort each under 5%. Held-out group prediction R2 above 0.8 with 2-fold cross-validation, above .6 on most tasks. Example: a group with Qwen2.5-72B (g = 119.9) cost 75% more but had ACI 9.7% lower than an internlm2.5-20b group (g = 92.1).
limits: 108 groups, half used for training. Group indicators are design variables defined by the authors (node degree and node ability), so the process effect is partly built in.
agent_relevance: Matching effort to ability (stronger agents at hub positions) beat adding a stronger model. This is a cheap, testable design rule, but it came from one framework.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) ACI factor paper
finding: Using predicted ACI as a regularizer improved unseen-task results of two topology optimizers by small amounts.
numbers: GPTSwarm and G-Designer, leave-one-task-out. Gains 1.1% to 12.3% (average 4.6% reported). Examples: GPTSwarm math 0.81 to 0.91 (12.3%); G-Designer commonsense 0.73 to 0.77 (5.5%); GPTSwarm coding 0.87 to 0.89; writing 0.88 to 0.89.
limits: No confidence intervals or seeds reported in the text I read. Gains of 1 to 2 points may be noise. Predicted ACI is built from the same group indicators.
agent_relevance: Small gains in one setting. Not enough to justify a c-style step in a single-agent scaffold.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) ACI factor paper, limitations section
finding: Authors' own caveats: one collaboration framework, groups under 10, mostly empirical rather than theory.
numbers: Limitations list three items: no theory of the mechanism, one framework (Du et al. 2024 debate), groups under 10 agents.
limits: They do not discuss the human-side disputes (Credé and Howardson, Bates and Gupta) in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Warns against importing the human c claim without the human dispute. Pair with b03 and b08.

source: Riedl (2025) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models, arXiv 2510.05174
finding: A different route: an information-theoretic test of whether LLM groups show synergy beyond their parts. Prompt design moved groups from aggregates toward collectives.
numbers: Guessing game with no direct communication. Conditions: control, persona, persona plus 'think about what other agents might do'. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Simple game. Models not named on the page I read. The authors avoid claiming human-like cognition.
agent_relevance: The prompt that made each agent model the others produced complementarity. Relevant to one agent simulating several roles, but weak evidence.

source: Fan et al. (2026) Towards a science of collective AI: LLM-based multi-agent systems, arXiv 2602.05289
finding: Position paper. Says LLM multi-agent work lacks a metric that separates real collaboration gain from extra compute, and proposes a gain metric.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. Proposes a collaboration gain metric and a factor library.
limits: Abstract only. Position paper, no experiments seen.
agent_relevance: Any multi-agent or c-style claim should be compared at equal compute. Our scaffold should also report gain per token.

source: Rowe, Hattie and Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses
finding: Reasons the reviewers give for caution: tasks are lab and contrived, order effects are rarely controlled, and the c battery differs from wisdom-of-crowds methods.
numbers: Groups of 2 to 6, batteries of about 6.3 tasks lasting 1 to 2 hours. Random allocation in 13 of 18 samples. Few studies randomised task order. 14 of 19 samples in labs; 11 of 18 in the USA.
limits: Authors' own review limits. Search ended November 2019.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions for c: short lab batteries, free-talking groups. Not tested on long, structured agent workflows.

source: Credé and Howardson (2017), press account
finding: The critics' explanations for the cross-task correlation: low effort or confusion in some groups, and individual answers being averaged without real collaboration.
numbers: Example: the brick task gave 10 minutes and a point per use. At least one team scored zero. The critic sees a task-to-task link as possible but untested under realistic team conditions.
limits: Press summary. Opinions of the critic, not measured here. Samples were students and paid community members.
agent_relevance: A few near-zero outlier runs can create an apparent general factor. In agent tests, check for failure runs that move all tasks together.

source: Synthesis of what changed performance, from Riedl 2021 and Zhou 2026
finding: The only lever-like results with numbers are correlational: process skill congruence, strategy, group social sensitivity, and (in LLM groups) stronger agents at hub positions.
numbers: Riedl 2021: 1 SD higher CI is about 18% (plus or minus 12%) higher task performance. Leave-one-out r = .40. Zhou 2026 LLM groups: skill congruence over 50% of importance. No randomised intervention that raised c itself was found in the sources read.
limits: Built only from the sources read here.
agent_relevance: Do not claim that a scaffold step raises collective intelligence. Test steps against task accuracy at equal compute.
